title: thermodynamic-latency-scratch-alex-moreno
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad to capture experiments exploring whether short-term GPU thermal throttling / power management jitter can explain sporadic p99/p999 latency spikes seen on long-running containers. Not a polished report — notes-to-self + commands + raw observations.

Hypothesis:
- When a GPU goes through modest temperature swings under steady CPU+I/O load, there are intermittent micro-pauses (kernel frequency scaling, driver resets, or power governor transitions) that show up as high tail latency for single-stream near-saturation workloads.
- These pauses correlate with period of long-ish sequences (>1024 tokens) and heavy KV cache activity (lots of attention cache reads).

Test matrix (summary):
- Hardware: GPC-64 (NVIDIA A10g-like allocation), 16GB host RAM, 32GB GPU memory. (VM flavor: rtx-serve-4x)
- OS/drivers: Ubuntu 20.04, NVIDIA driver 525.xx, CUDA 11.8
- Runtime: serving-runtime v0.9.12 (local branch thermal-tail-debug)
- Model: opt-6.7b quantized q4o-kv (same weights, two variants: KV cache enabled/disabled)
- Workload: synthetic client (wrk-lm) that creates single-stream sessions, sequence length distribution: 10% short (<=64), 70% medium (256-512), 20% long (1024-1536).
- Load points: 1. baseline light (qps 8) 2. steady high (qps 60) near single-GPU saturation 3. spike pattern: 60s high / 30s idle cycles for 30min total.
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 latency, GPU frequency (nvidia-smi polling 1s), GPU temp, power draw, kernel activity (nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps), system dmesg for driver resets.

Experiment commands (how I launched):
- start runtime: "./bin/serve --model opt-6.7b-q4o --kv-cache true --concurrency 1 --max-workers 4 --log-level debug --metrics-port 9100"
- client: "wrk-lm --rate=60 --duration=1800 --clients=60 --pattern=long-heavy.json --endpoint=http://127.0.0.1:8080/generate"
- gpu telemetry collector (simple loop):
  while true; do nvidia-smi --query-gpu=temperature.gpu,clocks.sm,power.draw --format=csv,noheader >> therm-run-$(date +%s).csv; sleep 1; done

Raw observations (session 2026-02-20 run A):
- Baseline (qps 8) stable: p99 ~ 210ms, p999 ~ 360ms. GPU temp flat at 51C.
- High steady (qps 60) sustained for 40m: median throughput maintained; p99 rose to 420ms and p999 jumped sporadically up to 1.2s but only 6 samples in 40m.
- Telemetry: GPU temp rose from 51C -> 74C during ramp. At times when p999 spikes occurred, GPU clock dropped by ~200MHz for 2-4s and power draw dropped by ~30W.
- dmesg: no full driver resets, but a handful of WARNs reporting "PCIe link power state change" and "power limit exceeded, throttling" at matching timestamps.
- When KV cache is disabled the p999 spikes reduce by ~60% in frequency (still present but smaller magnitude).

Follow-up run (2026-02-22 run B) with forced fan profile (if available) and higher power cap:
- Set power limit to +15W and forced fan 80% (via vendor tooling). Result: temps stabilized around 66C; p999 tail events reduced by ~80% and max p999 dropped to ~650ms.

Quick conclusions / working hypothesis:
1) There is strong evidence that short-lived GPU frequency reductions (thermally/power-triggered) align with observed ultra-tail latency spikes.
2) KV cache activity amplifies the impact (long sequences keep GPU active longer and amplify power draw -> triggers scaling).
3) Operational mitigations that look promising: slightly higher power caps for long-running latency-sensitive instances, pre-emptive fan profile adjustments, or a runtime knob to modestly limit continuous sequence length per worker to avoid steady high-power regimes.

Notes-to-self / caveats:
- This is not conclusive: correlation is strong but we need lower-level counters (driver perf APIs) to determine whether the clock drop is due to thermal throttling, power capping, or something else (PCIe link state).
- Need to cross-check with other GPU types (A100-like vs T4-like) — some fleets already use different governors.
- Check cloud provider telemetry for host-level interventions (OCI/EC2 host power policy).

Next experiments (priority list):
- Add fine-grained perf counters (nvmlEvent or CUPTI) and sync timestamps with our traces (trace-id propagation).
- Run identical workload on a smaller quantized model to see whether compute intensity correlates linearly with spike rate (if not, I/O or driver path might be contributing).
- Synthetic long-only run to isolate sequence length effect (all >1024).
- Test with container CPU pinning + isolated cgroups to rule out CPU-induced stalls.

Artifacts / files produced during this work: (local copies)
- therm-run-2026-02-20.csv
- client-latency-2026-02-20.jsonl (per-request traces)
- drm-dmesg-snippets-2026-02-20.log
- notes/thermal-tail-stacktrace-samples.txt

Slack/PR/Dashboard notes:
- Posted interim findings to #runtime-ops with spike timestamps; flagged JIRA-ENG-1423 for follow-up and attached therm CSV.
- Draft PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/789 (adds optional fan/power hints to launch config).

Quick TODO (for next few days):
- [ ] Instrument CUPTI collection in debug builds and run small 15m collection to capture clock/power transitions.
- [ ] Run power-cap / fan experiments across at least 3 GPUs in fleet to quantify variance.
- [ ] Draft a short runbook for on-call with simple mitigations (restart with power-hint, throttle long-seqs).

Random ideas (brainstorm):
- Could we implement a runtime-sensing controller that dynamically caps max seq length per worker when continuous high-power is detected (soft cap for latency tiers)?
- Explore a kernel that yields between attention layers for particularly long sequences to allow hardware to cooldown — might be controversial for throughput but could reduce tail spikes.

Closing note: this felt like a mixture of thermal/power and workload pattern. Worth prioritizing because tail spikes affect enterprise SLAs and are hard to reproduce in unit tests. Keep this doc rough; will refine once CUPTI traces exist.

-- Alex M. (notes kept for my personal flow; shareable with eng-serving-runtime)
